title: Seedless (1.51)
hook: the first chapter of the Yoga Sutras ends by letting go of the very last thing the mind holds

segments.voice: Yesterday: ritambhara, truth-bearing wisdom, the knowing that carries the truth and leaves a groove that blocks all the others. Did you meet one thing as if for the first time? Today, the last sutra of chapter one. Day four hundred forty-six.

A gardener clears a field. First the big weeds. Then the small ones. Then the seeds still lying in the soil, waiting to sprout. At last there's one seed left: the special one she planted on purpose, the one that crowded out all the weeds. The field is quiet and clean. And now, strangely, she lets that one go too. Not because it was bad. Because the field was the point all along. That's sutra 1.51, the last line of the first chapter.
screen: `THE BIG WEEDS, THE SMALL ONES.` → `ONE GOOD SEED LEFT.` → `SHE LETS THAT ONE GO TOO.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.51: tasyapi nirodhe sarva nirodhan nirbijah samadhih. When even that is stilled, everything being stilled, there is seedless absorption. Even that: the impression left by yesterday's truth-bearing wisdom, the last good groove in the mind. When it too goes quiet, there's nothing left that could sprout again. Nirbija: without seed. Vyasa explains that the mind then dissolves back into its source, and the seer, purusha, rests alone, pure and free. And that loops all the way back to the third sutra, fifteen days ago: then the seer rests in its own form. The first chapter is a circle. It began with the definition of yoga, and it ends with yoga complete. Look at the path the chapter walked. Atha, now. The seer. The five turnings. Practice and non-attachment. Samadhi with seed, and without. The born-free and the rest of us. Or, devotion to Ishvara. Om, repeated with its meaning. The nine obstacles. One thing. The four keys. Or the breath. Many doors. Mastery, small to large. The crystal taking the color. Truth-bearing wisdom. And seedless. Seventeen sessions, from now to nothing held. This chapter is called the Samadhi Pada, the part on absorption. Tomorrow begins the Sadhana Pada, the part on practice, which many teachers say was written for the rest of us: minds still busy, still scattered, still learning. It starts with three simple things.
screen: `EVEN THAT IS STILLED.` · `NIRBIJA: NOTHING LEFT TO SPROUT.` · `BACK TO 1.3: THE SEER RESTS.` · `SEVENTEEN SESSIONS, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `SEEDLESS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Choose one simple support, the breath, and rest on it for a while. Then, without forcing anything, loosen your grip on the breath too. Let it breathe itself, and don't hold on to it as an object. Just sit, holding nothing in particular, aware. If a thought comes, it's fine; let it go without picking up a new support. This isn't about reaching anything. It's a taste of letting go of even the good seed. The bell holds the time.
Seedless. Nirbija samadhi, sutra 1.51: when even the last good impression is stilled, nothing remains that could sprout, and the seer rests in itself.
Your line: nirbija. Today, after you finish something you did well, let it go completely, no replaying, no polishing, and notice the quiet that's left. Day four hundred forty-six.

screen: `DAY 446 COUNTS.` → `SAMADHI PADA, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: KRIYA YOGA — DISCIPLINE, STUDY, SURRENDER.`

howItsDone: In classical yoga, seedless samadhi is described as the culmination of practice, and students study the whole first chapter as a map from the definition of yoga in 1.2 to its completion in 1.51.

match.prompt: the Samadhi Pada, start to finish.
pairs: the seer rests in its own form

myth: seedless samadhi still rests on a subtle object
nirbija means no seed at all: even the last impression is stilled.
the first chapter ends where sutra 1.3 pointed: the seer resting in itself
Vyasa says the seer then rests alone, pure and free.
1.1 to 1.51, read in this path over seventeen sessions.

fork.setup: truth-bearing wisdom has cleared away every other impression. only its own remains. what does sutra 1.51 do with it?
options: keep it forever as the highest state.
replace it with a new seed.
fork.reveal: when even that is stilled, everything stilled, there is seedless samadhi. the last good seed goes too.

original.note: Sanskrit nirbīja: seedless. the samadhi with nothing left that could sprout again.

trapdoor: what you thought: seedless means empty, a blank.
what it means: the mind holds nothing, not even its best insight, and the seer rests in its own form.
what a scholar hears: 1.51 completes nirodha (1.2) and returns to 1.3; Vyasa says the mind dissolves into prakriti with its samskaras, and purusha abides alone, the kaivalya of the fourth chapter.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.1–1.3 (the definition; the seer rests in its own form)

notes: Close of the Samadhi Pada (days 430–446, 17 sessions): names the part's words and points to the Sadhana Pada.

'Many teachers say' the second chapter is for distracted minds: traditionally drawn from Vyasa's comment at the start of chapter two (the first for the settled mind, the second for the distracted). Confirm.
Vyasa on 1.51 summarized: the mind ceases with its impressions and the purusha, abiding in itself, is called pure, alone and free. Confirm wording.
